title: operator-fallthrough-shortpath-playbook
content:
Executive summary:

This is a working playbook for handling short-path/edge-level failovers that cause partial-region degradation and require operator-led fallthrough to warm-standby regions. It consolidates lessons from the Feb 2025 regional egress drift incident and lab experiments around KV prefill, DNS TTL choreography, and incremental weight-shifting. This doc is intended as an operator checklist + decision guide rather than a formal postmortem.

High-level goals:
- Minimize user-visible errors (5xx spikes, large latency tail) during regional degradation.
- Preserve KV cache hit-rate where possible and preseed warm-standby caches before bulk traffic flows.
- Avoid abrupt global routing changes; use short, observable steps for traffic shifts with clear rollback criteria.
- Make operator responsibilities clear: who flips weights, who watches telemetry, and who escalates.

Context and when to use this playbook:
- Use when a single region's edge or egress layer is showing sustained elevated 5xx, connection timeouts to edge POPs, or BGP/peering instability impacting >10% of user queries from that geo for >10 minutes.
- Not for full-region datacenter level failures (follow the regional-evacuation runbook). This is for cases where anycast path degradation or localized CDN/peering issues cause a significant subset of traffic to fail or experience a tail latency increase.

Quick TL;DR checklist (operator action):
1) Set incident bridge, notify SRE lead and oncall product manager.
2) Switch short TTL routing marker (see DNS step) to 30s.
3) Run KV preseed script to warm top-1k prefixes to warm-standby region(s).
4) Shift 5% weight to warm-standby, wait 60s, validate success criteria.
5) Iterate +5% every 90s up to target (30–50%).
6) If 5xx rate or error budget breaches in target region, rollback 10% immediately and escalate.
7) Once stable, increase DNS TTL to normal and open follow-ups.

Detailed timeline (example case from Feb 2025 exercise):
- 14:06 UTC: Edge telemetry shows per-POP retransmits rising from 0.6% to 3.4% in europe-west-1 POP subset. Origin reachability nominal.
- 14:10 UTC: 5xx rate on europe-west-1 customers crosses 1.2% (alert).
- 14:13 UTC: Operator bridge created; initial hypotheses: peering flap affecting short-paths, client route bouncing.
- 14:17 UTC: TTL lowered from 300->30 at global DNS control plane to accelerate client convergence for future weight changes.
- 14:21 UTC: KV preseed job run targeting warm-standby in europe-north-1 for top-1k keys from active traffic sample.
- 14:25 UTC: First weight shift +5% to europe-north-1; monitoring dashboards show reduced 5xx in user cohort after ~40s.
- 14:36 UTC: Iterated to 30% weight; observed KV miss rate in europe-north-1 improve from 72% miss-> 21% miss as preseed finished.
- 15:10 UTC: Metrics stabilized; DNS TTL raised back to 120.

Observability and success criteria (what to watch closely):
- 5xx/sec per-region and per-route (primary signal). Trigger high priority if sustained >0.5% absolute increase over baseline for 5+ minutes.
- Tail latency (p95/p99) — watch for sudden spikes when shifting weights.
- KV cache miss rate in warm region: target <30% before moving >25% weight. If miss rate >50%, throttle weight increases and consider re-running preseed.
- Connection error rates (timeouts, TLS handshake failures) per egress POP.
- BGP flaps and peer session resets (from network team). If persistent, consider peering-level mitigation instead of traffic shift.

Operator play actions (step-by-step):
1) Bridge & comms: create incident bridge, add network, infra, and product PM reps. Update status page if customer-facing.
2) Set DNS TTL to 30s in control plane and confirm propagation window. Rationale: short TTL reduces time-to-converge for subsequent weight adjustments and client re-resolve behavior. Note: short TTLs increase DNS query volume — watch resolver QPS.
3) Run kv-prefill script (scripts/kv_prefill.py) against chosen warm-standby region with sample of hot prefixes derived from last 15 minutes. Check logs for prefill success (approx 95% pass threshold).
4) Validate warm-standby health: internal health checks green, model load OK, instance counts within target.
5) Apply traffic weight increment (operator console) +5% to standby, observe for 60–90s.
6) Check p50/p95/p99 latency and 5xx for both primary and standby cohorts. If errors increase in standby, immediately rollback 10% and call network lead.
7) Continue increments until target weight reached or until primary region error rate falls under baseline.
8) After stabilization for 30 minutes, revert DNS TTL to normal (recommended 120–300s). If traffic remains with high miss rates, schedule a background prefill to continue improving cache hit ratio.

Rollback criteria (explicit):
- Any single increment leads to >=0.2% absolute increase in global 5xx for 3 consecutive samples (1-min sampling).
- Standby region p99 latency > 2x primary p99 for 2 samples or more.
- Persistent KV miss rate >60% in standby after two prefill attempts.
- Network layer signals (BGP peer down) in standby region within the shift window.

Runbook caveats & operator notes:
- DNS TTL changes are blunt instruments. In cases where clients obey long-cached records (ISP caching) you may not see immediate movement. Balance TTL lowering with expected DNS query amplification.
- Preseeding costs: prefill will read hot keys from origin which can raise origin load. Rate-limit prefill job and use sampling to avoid origin overload.
- Some clients maintain sticky connections; weight shift will be gradual. Expect a 1–3 minute lag for steady state.
- If the cause is BGP or peering flap, shifting traffic may mask root cause and increase pressure on alternate peers. Coordinate with network team for peering-level mitigation.

Playbook automation candidates (post-incident work):
- Automate kv-prefill trigger when a region's 5xx crosses threshold and traffic is being rebalanced.
- Add automated small-step weight-shifts with safety checks and automated rollback on metric regressions.
- Dashboarding: add a single-pane operator view that shows per-region kv-miss, 5xx, p99, weight percentages, DNS TTL, and last prefill timestamp.

Follow-ups and action items (owners & ETA):
- Rina: add prefill cost-mode to scripts so we can simulate without origin writes (ETA: 2025-03-10).
- Marcus: implement single-pane dashboard prototype for fallthrough shifts (ETA: 2025-03-17).
- Aisha: write a small automation PR to propose +5% incremental shifts with rollback logic (draft PR: github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/1893) (ETA: 2025-03-07).
- Network: evaluate peering resiliency in europe-west POPs and provide mitigation play (owner: Jon, ETA: 2025-03-20).

Open questions and unresolved risks:
- How does long-lived client caching (mobile carriers) affect our ability to move traffic quickly? Need empirical sampling per carrier to quantify.
- What SLO adjustments are appropriate to allow short TTL experiments in production without creating alert storms?
- Can we rely on warm-standby regions' KV capacity at large scale (beyond top-1k prefixes)? We need capacity planning for prefill at 10–50% traffic scenarios.

Appendix: operator commands and snippets
- Lower TTL (control plane CLI): infra dns set-ttl --zone=global --value=30
- Run kv prefiller (example): python3 scripts/kv_prefill.py --source-sample=15m --top-n=1000 --target-region=europe-north-1 --rate-limit=200qps
- Increment weight (operator console): route-manager set-weight --route=global-api --region=europe-north-1 --delta=+5
- Monitor quick query: curl -sS "https://internal-monitoring/api/region-stats?region=europe-west-1"

Retrospective notes (informal):
- Preseeding was the single biggest win in our lab run; without it, the standby experienced very high initial miss rates causing latency spikes that negated the benefit of shifting.
- Short TTL during shifts reduced the time for clients to re-resolve, but we saw a measurable spike in DNS QPS on resolvers — need to ensure upstream resolver quotas are known.
- Operator anxiety point: decision to lower TTL often feels risky; make sure customer-facing comms are prepped before TTL changes.

If you have additions or corrections, leave inline comments here or ping on #sre-ops.

-- doc owner: Aisha Martinez (eng-sre)
